papers.title: Multi-Modal Wearable and Biological Data Integration Reveals Physiological Signatures of Weight Variation in Overweight and Obese Adults: An AI4Food Machine Learning Study
papers.abstract: This study is part of the AI4Food project, which aims to identify the physiological and behavioral factors influencing weight variation in overweight and obese individuals through integrative analysis of multi-source data. A 30-day crossover intervention was conducted on 93 participants at IMDEA Nutrition Institute, combining a traditional phase (questionnaires, food diaries) and a digital phase (Fitbit Sense Smartwatch, FreeStyle Libre 2 glucose sensor). The collected data encompassed sleep, glucose, skin temperature, nutrition, and gut microbiome information. After rigorous preprocessing and alignment by intervention days, unsupervised clustering, association analysis, and machine learning models were applied to uncover physiological patterns linked to weight dynamics. Results showed greater weight reduction during the digital phase in Group 2, while between-group differences were not significant. Significant associations were observed between nocturnal respiratory rate, skin temperature, and weight variation. Under participant-level five-fold cross-validation, Random Forest models achieved mean accuracies of 64.3% for thermoregulation and 61.7% for glucose phenotype prediction, with RMSSD, restlessness, and nocturnal respiratory rate among the most influential predictors. In contrast, microbiome composition remained almost stable over the short intervention period. These findings support the potential of AI-driven integration of wearable and nutritional data to stratify metabolic phenotypes and advance personalized nutrition strategies in obesity management.

papers.title: Hypoxic Burden Predicts Symptomatic but Not Sleep Architecture Response to CPAP Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) remains the standard metric for assessing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity, although it does not fully capture the physiological consequences of respiratory events. Hypoxic burden (HB), which integrates the frequency, depth, and duration of oxygen desaturations, has been proposed as a more comprehensive measure of OSA-related hypoxic stress. This study compared the prognostic value of HB and AHI for subjective and objective treatment outcomes in patients undergoing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. Data from 412 patients with OSA who underwent diagnostic and CPAP-treated polysomnography were analyzed, including 52 patients with available follow-up questionnaires. HB was calculated using a validated event-based algorithm. Multivariable regression models were used to predict patient-reported outcomes and changes in sleep architecture, adjusted for age, sex and body mass index. HB consistently demonstrated stronger associations with symptomatic outcomes than AHI. Models including HB showed improved model fit and explained variance. HB remained independently associated with lower follow-up fatigue and better sleep quality after adjustment for AHI. In contrast, AHI was the dominant predictor of objective sleep architecture improvements, including increases in N3 sleep, reductions in N1 sleep, and reductions in arousal index. HB provided additional independent information only for changes in arousal burden. These findings suggest that HB and AHI capture complementary dimensions of OSA severity. While AHI primarily reflects sleep fragmentation and physiological response to CPAP, HB appears more closely related to subjective treatment benefit. Incorporating HB alongside AHI may improve clinical phenotyping and prediction of treatment response in OSA.

papers.title: Electric and Magnetic Source Imaging in Epilepsy: Anatomical Insights from Realistic Simulations
papers.abstract: Neurosurgery is an effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), but its success depends on the accurate delineation of the epileptogenic focus, approximated noninvasively by electric and magnetic source imaging (ESI/MSI) of high-density electroencephalography (HD-EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). These modalities have distinct sensitivity profiles; consequently, epileptiform activity detected by one modality may remain undetected by the other. However, the implications of these differences for spike detectability and localization accuracy, and the added value of combined electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), remain insufficiently characterized under clinically realistic conditions. Here, we characterize HD-EEG and MEG sensitivity profiles and compare ESI, MSI, and EMSI, using realistic simulations with known ground truth. We generated HD-EEG and MEG datasets from cortical, insular, and hippocampal sources across multiple orientations, activated using patient-derived intracranial EEG spike waveforms. Spike sensitivity and localization accuracy were evaluated using dipole scanning, dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV). EEG demonstrated higher spike detection rates and sensitivity for radially cortical sources at gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms (p<0.001), while MEG detected more spikes from tangential cortical sources along sulcal walls (p<0.001). MSI localized tangential sources more accurately than ESI across all methods (p<0.001), while dipole scanning outperformed dSPM and LCMV for cortical and insular sources (p<0.001). EMSI outperformed ESI (p<0.001) but did not improve localization over MSI. These findings suggest that complementary anatomical sensitivities of HD-EEG and MEG may improve epileptogenic source characterization, supporting simultaneous acquisition during the presurgical evaluation of patients with DRE.

papers.title: Optimized phase-targeted auditory stimulation reduces nocturnal spikes in childhood epilepsies
papers.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges, so called spikes, are often strongly activated during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in childhood epilepsies. In children with pronounced spike activation during NREM - sleep, spike burden can be associated with lifelong impaired cognitive functions. This spike activation is also related to alterations in sleep oscillations, specifically slow waves and spindles, which play essential roles in brain maintenance and maturation. These observations suggest that spikes may disrupt sleep-dependent brain processes that are critical for the development of cognitive functions. Phase-targeted auditory stimulation during NREM sleep delivers brief, non-arousing tones at specific phases of ongoing slow waves to modulate sleep oscillations. Recently, our group showed that isolated, less frequent, and thus less expected, tones engage widespread thalamocortical networks, whereas repetitive, regular trains of tones promote habituation and engage more local corticocortical networks. In this study, we use these contrasting stimulation patterns for a targeted modulation of sleep oscillations and examine their interaction with epileptic spikes. In an initial exploratory study (N = 10; age range: 7.3 - 16.2 years), we used a within-night block design to directly compare responses to the different stimulation patterns. Isolated tones delivered at long interstimulus intervals induced a transient increase in spike rate, whereas down-phase stimulation delivered in trains at short, regular intervals was associated with a significant reduction. We subsequently optimized the train-based paradigm and evaluated stimulation delivered throughout the night in a proof-of-concept study using a counterbalanced, between-night design (N = 5; age range: 4.4 - 10.7 years). Spike density decreased locally in all patients, providing convergent evidence for the effects observed in the exploratory study. With this mechanistically guided approach, we demonstrate that repetitive down-phase auditory stimulation of slow waves results in a local reduction of epileptic spikes. This framework may provide a rational basis for targeted interventions aimed at reducing spikes and related cognitive impairments.

papers.title: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
papers.abstract: Importance: Cognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal a-synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. Objective: To characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). Design: Longitudinal cohort study using Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. Setting: Multicenter cohort. Participants: Healthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). Exposures: NSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and Measures: Cognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE {varepsilon}4 status. Results: Among 3031 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.6 [7.0] years; 1322 female [43.6%]), prodromal NSD participants had lower baseline verbal-memory performance than HC (adjusted difference, -0.20 SD; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.07; adjusted P = .007); NSD-negative genetic carriers did not differ from HC. No other cognitive domain was lower than HC at baseline or longitudinally. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, verbal-memory trajectory differed from HC over 4 years (P = .009), whereas in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not (P = .62); the baseline difference persisted (adjusted difference, -0.28 SD; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.10; P = .003). Adjusted MCI probability increased from 10.2% to 15.1% in prodromal NSD, compared with 8.4% to 5.0% in HC and 13.4% to 17.7% in PD. The increase was greater than in HC (ratio of annual odds ratios, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.58; adjusted P = .04) but not PD (P = .62). Conclusions and Relevance: Prodromal NSD was associated with modestly lower verbal memory and increasing MCI probability relative to HC, without lower performance in other cognitive domains. The baseline verbal-memory difference was robust, whereas the longitudinal trajectory finding was not reproduced in the smaller age-matched sensitivity subset.

papers.title: Natural History Of Oral Human Papillomavirus In Nigerian Mothers And Youth With And Without HIV: A Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Objectives: HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is rising, yet the natural history of oral-HPV, particularly persistence remains poorly characterized in sub-Saharan Africa and in people living with HIV (PLWH). We characterized oral HPV prevalence, incident detection, persistence, and clearance over four visits in a Nigerian mother-youth cohort with and without HIV and quantified the genotype distribution relative to vaccine coverage. Methods: Within the prospective HOMINY cohort, 1075 participants (404 mothers and 671 youth) were followed across four visits at 6-month intervals. Oral rinses were genotyped with the Seegene Allplex HPV28 assay (28 genotypes). Persistence was defined as detection at [≥]2 visit (not necessarily consecutive), with type-specific and visit 2-4 sensitivity definitions. We used modified-Poisson models for visit-level detection, Markov multistate models for acquisition and clearance, and a permutation test for mother-youth genotype concordance. Results: Oral HPV was detected at least once in 112 participants (10.4% overall; 11.1% mothers and 10% youth); incident detection was around 6% in both groups. Persistence was uncommon (1.9%), and only 3 had oral HPV DNA detected at all four visits. Clearance predominated across every visit interval. In Markov models, clearance was slower in PLWH (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.77) with no difference in acquisition (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.5). Persistence concentrated among PLWH. Only 31.2% of ever-positive participants carried a Gardasil-9 preventable strain of HPV; HPV16 and HPV39 were most frequent. Mother-youth genotype concordance exceeded chance (permutation p =0.009). Conclusion: Oral HPV was common but transient; persistence was confined to a small PLWH minority and was dominated by high-risk non-vaccine genotypes, leaving most infections beyond the reach of current vaccines.

papers.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Brief Health Chatbot Acceptability Scale (CAS): A Pilot Study
papers.abstract: Background. Conversational agents (chatbots) are increasingly used to deliver health information to middle-aged and older adults, a population in which the determinants of technology acceptance are known to diverge from those of younger users. However, acceptability is inconsistently defined and typically measured with ad hoc, unvalidated instruments. The psychometrically sound chatbot measures that exist assess usability rather than acceptability or were validated in student samples. Objective. To develop and conduct an initial psychometric evaluation of a brief, 10-item health chatbot acceptance measure grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Methods. Twenty adults (mean age = 52.8 years, range 28-81; 85% aged 40 or older; 75% female) enrolled in a sleep-application pilot usability study completed the 10 candidate items, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and sleep measures (PROMIS Sleep Disturbance 8a; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). We examined item performance, internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), dimensionality (exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation), and convergent validity (correlations with the SUS). Results. A two-factor structure emerged and was invariant across rotation methods, resulting in an Information Quality factor and an Acceptance factor (interfactor r = .39). All items loaded [≥] .60 on their primary factor; mean communality was .83. Subscale reliabilities were high (Information Quality = .96; Acceptance = .94; full scale = .93). Both subscales correlated with the SUS in the expected direction (r = .69 and r = .59), providing preliminary support for convergent validity. Conclusions. The measure shows a coherent and theory-consistent two-factor structure and shows preliminary evidence of reliability and convergent validity. Given the small pilot sample, these results must be viewed as provisional but identify the measure as a candidate for formal validation in a larger, independent sample.

papers.title: Music-Synchronized Gamma Light Stimulation Strengthens Theta-Gamma Coupling in Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: Results from a Randomized Feasibility Trial
papers.abstract: Noninvasive clinical innovations for restoring gamma activity via sound and light stimulation have the potential to improve memory and cognitive abilities in Alzheimer's disease. We assessed whether pairing music with theta- and gamma-band light changes memory-supporting neural dynamics, and whether those changes track cognition. In an ongoing randomized feasibility trial, 38 older adults with cognitive impairment completed eight weeks of an audiovisual intervention. The treatment group (n = 19) listened to self-selected music while viewing light stimulation that consisted of a 39-Hz gamma-band signal modulated by delta- and theta-band musical rhythms. The control group (n = 19) listened to podcasts while viewing synchronized lights without the gamma frequency (delta-band only). Before and after the 8-week intervention, participants completed a face-name association task and the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive (ADAS-Cog). Individuals in the treatment group showed significant improvements on a face-name association task and the ADAS-Cog. Cluster-based permutation testing showed a larger increase in phase-amplitude coupling between acoustic theta phase and frontal EEG gamma amplitude in the treatment group compared to the control group. Across participants, increases in stimulus-driven theta to EEG-gamma phase-amplitude coupling were associated with improvements in memory. These preliminary results suggest that theta-gamma stimulation delivered through music and lights strengthens cross-frequency coupling, and may correspondingly strengthen associative memory.
